issues.description: The problem statement and UML explicitly require Farm.animals to be a List<Animal> implemented using an ArrayList and initialized in a no-arg constructor, but the solution implements the animals collection as a Queue<Animal> backed by a LinkedList and exposes getter/setter with Queue<Animal>. This mismatches the specified attribute type and collection implementation, which can confuse students about the required type and API to use (List vs Queue) and about how to initialize the collection.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the Farm class use the collection type specified in the problem statement: change the animals field type to List<Animal>, initialize it as a new ArrayList<>() in the no-arg constructor, and update the getter and setter signatures to use List<Animal>. Adjust addAnimal to use animals.add(a) and keep iteration logic unchanged. Alternatively, update the problem description to accept a Queue/LinkedList if that design is preferred, but ensure consistency across statement, template, and solution.

issues.description: The problem statement explicitly defines the Farm's animal collection as a List<Animal> and instructs to initialize it using an ArrayList in the no-arg constructor, but the solution uses a Queue<Animal> backed by a LinkedList (attribute name 'animals' is the same). This mismatches the collection type described in the assignment and may confuse students who are instructed to implement an ArrayList-based List; they may be unable to directly map the problem instructions to the solution's implementation choice.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the solution with the problem instructions by using the same collection type: declare the attribute as List<Animal> animals and initialize it with new ArrayList<>() in the no-argument constructor (update imports to java.util.List and java.util.ArrayList). Alternatively, adjust the problem statement to accept a Queue/LinkedList if that design is intentional, but keep wording consistent across artifacts.
